title: Box Office Boom: “You Can See Everything” Ranks 2nd Biggest U.S. Documentary Ever with $80 Million
body:
The documentary “You Can See Everything,” chronicling the rise and fall of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has surged past the $80 million mark in North American box‑office receipts after just four weekends, making it the second‑highest‑grossing documentary ever released in the United States. The A24‑distributed film’s unprecedented performance not only eclipses the previous record‑holder but also signals a growing appetite for true‑crime storytelling that blends investigative journalism with cinematic flair.

From its limited debut in early May, the film opened to a modest $3.1 million in 1,200 theaters, a figure that would have seemed respectable for a nonfiction feature but modest by Hollywood standards. Yet word‑of‑mouth, amplified by social media buzz and a cascade of positive reviews, propelled the documentary into a rare “sleeper hit” trajectory. By its second weekend, the film had expanded to over 2,500 screens, adding $12 million to its tally, and it maintained a strong per‑theater average that outpaced many mainstream releases. The cumulative $80 million comes at a time when theatrical attendance remains uneven, underscoring the documentary’s cross‑demographic resonance.

Industry analysts attribute the film’s success to several converging factors. First, the Theranos saga remains fresh in the public consciousness, having been revisited through a popular limited series and numerous podcasts. “You Can See Everything” offers a fresh, unvarnished perspective, featuring never‑before‑seen footage, exclusive interviews with former employees, and a narrative structure that reads like a courtroom thriller. Second, A24’s brand reputation for championing bold, auteur‑driven projects has cultivated a loyal audience that trusts the studio’s curatorial choices. Finally, the documentary’s release strategy—pairing a limited opening with an aggressive expansion plan—mirrored the rollout of past breakout hits such as “Won’t You Be My Neighbor?” and “Free Solo,” demonstrating that documentaries can thrive when given the same distribution muscle as narrative features.

The financial milestone also redefines the commercial viability of documentary filmmaking. Historically, documentaries have occupied a niche market, often relegated to art‑house cinemas or streaming platforms. “You Can See Everything” joins a short list of nonfiction titles that have cracked the eight‑figure barrier, alongside “Fahrenheit 9/11,” “March of the Penguins,” and the recent “American Factory.” Its success may encourage studios to invest more heavily in high‑production‑value documentaries, allocate larger marketing budgets, and pursue wider theatrical releases, potentially reshaping the landscape for nonfiction cinema.

Critics have praised the film for its meticulous editing, which weaves together courtroom testimonies, internal company memos, and personal moments that humanize the central figures without absolving them. Director Ava Patel’s approach—eschewing sensationalism in favor of a methodical, almost forensic storytelling style—has been highlighted as a key differentiator from the more dramatized portrayals seen on television. The documentary’s ability to maintain narrative tension while delivering factual rigor has set a new benchmark for the genre, suggesting that audiences are hungry for content that respects both intelligence and entertainment.

Looking ahead, “You Can See Everything” is poised to continue its ascent as it heads into its fifth weekend, with projections indicating it could breach the $100 million threshold—a feat never before achieved by a documentary in the U.S. market. Its performance may inspire a wave of investigative documentaries tackling contemporary scandals, from tech ethics to political corruption, with studios more willing to back ambitious projects. As the line between documentary and mainstream cinema blurs, the success of “You Can See Everything” could herald a new era where factual storytelling commands the same box‑office clout as blockbuster franchises, reshaping audience expectations and industry economics alike.
